plan.topic: Breakfast on tirzepatide when you're barely hungry: why a small, protein-forward breakfast helps, with 2 concrete examples
plan.angle: Question: 'Not hungry in the morning on tirzepatide? Do you still need breakfast?' Honest answer: there's no rule that you must eat breakfast. But when appetite is low all day, a small protein-forward breakfast is one easy way to get closer to enough protein. Credit only 'get enough protein' (and, where relevant, the nausea tip about the first few days) to the 2025 ACLM/ASN/OMA/TOS joint advisory. 'Protein food first', small portions and eating slowly are our own tips, with no tag. Two examples, with 'grams vary by brand, check the label': a small pot of plain Greek yogurt (about 15–20 grams of protein, per the label) or 2 eggs (about 12 grams, per the label/USDA). Kidney caveat: 'If you have kidney disease, ask your clinician how much protein is right for you.' One GI line: if food sits heavily or nausea is bad, smaller and blander portions may sit better; persistent vomiting or severe belly pain means calling your prescriber. No calorie or restriction talk. 'Not personal advice' plus the prescriber line. No Exp F line. Last line: 'Full breakdown on our channel, link in the description.'
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide Breakfast When You're Not Hungry
plan.why: Exp D funnel to the live What to Eat and Protein long-forms (Protein had our fastest Lane A start). It rides the EatingWell breakfast story from Nov 1. | fact-check: This is a safe, useful funnel topic for What to Eat and Protein. The 2025 joint advisory (ACLM/ASN/OMA/TOS, Mozaffarian et al.) supports eating enough protein and nutrient-dense foods while on GLP-1 medicines. Per the craft notes, its quotable content is enough protein, strength training at least 3 times a week, and avoiding fatty or high-fibre foods in the first few days to ease nausea. I could not confirm that it says 'eat your protein food first', and nothing suggests it says to eat breakfast. Credit only what it prints. Framing: the answer must not tell people to eat when they aren't hungry as a rule, or suggest that skipping breakfast is harmful. Present it as one option for hitting daily protein when appetite is low. Gram counts must come from a food label and be phrased 'about, as on the label', because they vary by brand. Avoid calorie talk, as planned.

package.title: Tirzepatide: No Appetite for Breakfast? #shorts
package.description:
Barely hungry on tirzepatide in the morning? Breakfast isn't required, but protein can be easy to miss. Small options: plain, strained Greek yogurt (often 15–20g, check your label) or 2 large eggs (about 12g). Severe belly pain that won't go away? Call your prescriber right away. On insulin or a sulfonylurea, ask your prescriber before skipping meals. Kidney disease? Ask your clinician how much protein is right for you.
Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
Sources: Mozaffarian et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2025 (joint GLP-1 nutrition advisory); FDA Nutrition Facts Label guide.
#Tirzepatide #GLP1 #ProteinFirst

social.instagram_caption:
No morning appetite on tirzepatide? No guilt here — breakfast isn't required.

But here's the catch: with low appetite all day, protein and overall food can be easy to miss.

A 2025 joint advisory on GLP-1 medicines says to get enough protein. Two easy, small ways to do that:
• A single-serve pot of plain, strained Greek yogurt — often 15 to 20 grams of protein (check your label)
• Two large eggs — about 12 grams (bigger or smaller eggs change that, so check the carton)

Protein first, small portions, eat slowly. Feeling queasy? Smaller, blander bites may sit better.

Save this for your next low-appetite morning.

Severe belly pain that won't go away (with or without vomiting)? Call your prescriber right away. On insulin or a sulfonylurea for diabetes? Skipping meals can raise the risk of low blood sugar, so ask your prescriber first. Kidney disease? Ask your clinician how much protein is right for you.

#Tirzepatide #GLP1 #ProteinFirst

Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary:
This Short is accurate and safe. It passes with five small fixes.

What checks out:
- **Joint advisory (s1):** the 2025 GLP-1 nutrition advisory exists. It's in AJCN 122(1):344–367, published online 30 May 2025 (July 2025 issue), and it does stress getting enough protein.
- **Belly-pain line (scene 7):** it matches the Zepbound Medication Guide's pancreatitis warning wording. The script leaves out the guide's "stop using" instruction, which is right for our no-stopping rule.
- **Low blood sugar line (scene 8):** the warning about insulin or a sulfonylurea matches the label.
- **Egg figure:** USDA SR Legacy 171287 gives 12.6 g protein per 100 g. A large egg is about 50 g, so 2 large eggs come to about 12.6 g, and "about twelve grams" holds.
- **Yogurt figure:** USDA nonfat plain Greek yogurt has about 10.2 g protein per 100 g. A 150–170 g pot comes to roughly 15–17 g. Common US pots list 15–18 g and some high-protein lines list 20 g, so "often fifteen to twenty… check your label" is acceptable. The USDA entry itself only backs the lower part of that range.
- **Safety and rules:** the safety caveats are all there (diabetes medicines and low blood sugar, kidney disease and protein, belly pain). There's no dosing, no extreme-diet nudge, a neutral mascot on the risk line, the disclaimer, the prescriber line and the correct funnel CTA.

What needs a fix:
- Neither USDA FoodData Central link (s2, s5) opened when I tried it (HTTP 404). Replace them or confirm they work before anything goes into a public field.
- The rest are wording and tagging fixes, listed below.

issues.problem: Both URLs came back HTTP 404 when I fetched them, so I couldn't confirm they work. The craft notes don't allow unreachable links in the source list. The nutrient values themselves are correct: egg 12.6 g/100 g, nonfat Greek yogurt about 10.2 g/100 g.
issues.fix: Before publishing, open both links in a browser. If they don't load, use the FoodData Central search page record or the USDA API record for FDC 171287 and 170903, or drop s2 and s5 from the public description and keep s3 (FDA Nutrition Facts Label page, current as of 03/05/2024).

issues.claim: Protein, single-serve plain strained Greek yogurt (150–170 g; varies by brand): 15–20 g
issues.problem: At 10.2 g per 100 g, the cited USDA entry gives about 15–17 g for 150–170 g. The 20 g upper end comes from brand labels, not from s5. The 'varies by brand' hedge covers it, but the label credits USDA without saying what USDA actually supports.
issues.fix: Change stat_label to: "Protein, single-serve plain strained Greek yogurt (150–170 g pot; varies by brand, check label)". Keep the narration as written.

issues.claim: Or two large eggs: about twelve grams.
issues.problem: USDA gives 12.6 g for 2 large eggs (2 × 50 g). 'About twelve' is acceptable and slightly understates it, which is the safer direction. No change is strictly needed.
issues.fix: Optional: "Or two large eggs: about twelve to thirteen grams." with on_screen_text "2 large eggs: ~12–13 g". Otherwise leave it as is.

issues.claim: On insulin or a sulfonylurea for diabetes? Skipping meals can raise the risk of low blood sugar
issues.problem: The scene has no source tag, but the label and Medication Guide do support a higher low-blood-sugar risk when Zepbound is used with insulin or a sulfonylurea. 'Skipping meals' and the kidney line are general safety lines and need no tag.
issues.fix: Set source_ids to ["s4"] (Zepbound label, hypoglycaemia with insulin or a sulfonylurea). Keep the narration unchanged.

issues.claim: source_ids ["s4b", "s4"] on a line that also contains our own 'blander bites' tip
issues.problem: The tags need to cover only the belly-pain sentence, not the 'smaller, blander bites' tip, which is our own advice. The retention note already says this. Make sure the description and captions don't credit the blander-bites tip to Lilly or the label.
issues.fix: Leave the tags as they are. In the description sources, credit s4b only for: "severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away, with or without vomiting: call your healthcare provider right away".
